summary: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is an island nation in the eastern Caribbean made up of the island of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines archipelago, known for its volcano, yachting destinations and arrowroot industry.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Britain acquired Saint Vincent after the 1763 Treaty of Paris, and the colonists brought Anglicanism; in 1787 the Methodist Thomas Coke began preaching to African slaves, and Protestantism gradually became the mainstream. Residents of African descent blended West African beliefs to develop the Spiritual Baptists (commonly called "Shakers"), who were banned by colonial law in 1912 and not freed from the ban until 1965. In recent decades Pentecostals and Seventh-day Adventists have grown rapidly, and Protestant denominations together account for three quarters of the population.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholic influence comes partly from the brief French occupation of 1779-1783 and French settlers, and partly from the indentured laborers from the Portuguese island of Madeira, mostly Catholics, who were recruited after 1845 to work on plantations. Because the Anglican church was dominant under British rule, Catholicism has always remained a minority denomination.

ranking.name: Rastafari
ranking.description: The Rastafari movement originated in Jamaica in the 1930s, venerating Ethiopian Emperor Haile Selassie, crowned in 1930, as a sacred figure and stressing African identity and return to Africa. In the 1970s, as reggae music became popular in the eastern Caribbean, Rastafari belief spread to Saint Vincent; its followers have long faced social discrimination and legal problems related to cannabis, and though few in number they have a clear cultural influence.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Saint Vincentian society is strongly religious, and the church plays an important role in community, education and family life; attending church on Sundays is still a common habit. Few people therefore state clearly that they have no religion, mainly young people affected by secularization in towns such as the capital, Kingstown.

religion.background: The indigenous people of Saint Vincent were the Caribs and the Garifuna, formed through later intermixture with escaped African slaves; they resisted European colonization for a long time, and in 1797 after the Second Carib War the British exiled several thousand Garifuna to the island of Roatán in Central America. British colonists brought Anglicanism, while Methodists preached among the slaves, and residents of African descent developed syncretic faiths such as the Spiritual Baptists. After independence in 1979 the constitution guaranteed freedom of religion; today Protestant denominations are the mainstream, and new movements such as Rastafari also have some influence.

ranking.name: Vincentian Creole English
ranking.description: Vincentian Creole English is a language developed on 18th-century plantations by African slaves on the basis of English, blending the grammar and pronunciation of West African languages and absorbing some vocabulary from French and the indigenous Caribbean languages. It is the language of the home, the street and daily communication, and almost all Vincentians speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English has been the language of administration and education since British colonization in 1763, and after independence in 1979 it remains the sole official language, used in government, the courts, schools and the media. Most people speak Creole English in daily life and switch to standard English only on formal occasions, creating a linguistic environment in which the two are used side by side.

language.history: The indigenous people of Saint Vincent spoke Carib, while the Garifuna developed Garifuna, a language that blended Arawak, Carib and African languages; after most of the Garifuna were exiled in 1797, this language nearly disappeared on the island. African slaves on British colonial plantations formed an English-based creole, and the brief French rule also left some vocabulary. Today standard English is the official language, while Vincentian Creole English is the language of daily life.

ranking.name: Roasted breadfruit with fried jackfish
ranking.description: Whole breadfruit is roasted over charcoal until the skin is blackened, then peeled and sliced and served with crisply fried jackfish (jack) and a tomato and onion sauce; it is the national dish of Saint Vincent.
ranking.history: In 1793 the British naval officer William Bligh, aboard HMS Providence, brought breadfruit seedlings from Tahiti and planted them in the Saint Vincent Botanic Gardens, founded in 1765, with the aim of providing cheap food for plantation slaves; the garden is also one of the oldest botanic gardens in the Western Hemisphere. Breadfruit later became the staple of Vincentians, and paired with jackfish caught offshore it became the national dish. The local Breadfruit Festival also features this dish as its star.

ranking.name: Callaloo
ranking.description: A thick green soup in which dasheen (taro) leaves, okra, onions and coconut milk are stewed and then blended, sometimes with crab or salted meat added for flavor.
ranking.history: Callaloo derives from the cooking tradition of enslaved West Africans; stews of okra and leafy greens are very common in West Africa, and after being brought to the Caribbean they merged with the locally grown dasheen taro. On Saint Vincent and the islands of the eastern Caribbean, it is a common soup at Sunday family lunches. Taro leaves are nutritious and easy to grow, which made this soup an important source of nutrition for slaves and farmers in the plantation era.

ranking.name: Pelau
ranking.description: Sugar is first browned into caramel to color the chicken, then rice, pigeon peas, coconut milk and herbs are added and simmered together; it tastes salty, sweet and richly fragrant and is a one-pot dish.
ranking.history: The name and method of pelau derive from the "pilaf" of the Middle East and South Asia, and came with the Indian indentured laborers who reached the eastern Caribbean in the late 19th century; the technique of burning sugar to color meat is thought to come from African culinary tradition. One pot can feed many people, so it is very popular at family gatherings, beach picnics and festive parties on Saint Vincent.

ranking.name: Saltfish
ranking.description: Salted dried cod is soaked in water to remove the salt and sautéed with onions, tomatoes, sweet peppers and chili peppers, often served for breakfast with roasted breadfruit, fried dough (bakes) or boiled bananas.
ranking.history: Salt cod was a product of the "triangular trade" of the 17th-19th centuries: fish catches from Newfoundland and New England were salted and shipped to the Caribbean as a cheap, long-keeping source of protein for plantation slaves, and the return voyage carried back cane sugar and molasses. After slavery was abolished, saltfish remained in the Caribbean diet and became the most common breakfast accompaniment in Saint Vincent and the main ingredient of fish cakes.

ranking.name: Arrowroot
ranking.description: A fine white starch extracted from the rhizomes of the arrowroot plant, used for thickening, making biscuits and baby food, and often used to make traditional desserts and puddings.
ranking.history: Arrowroot is a plant that the indigenous Caribbean people used from early times, and it was planted on a large scale on Saint Vincent in the colonial period. In the early 20th century Saint Vincent was the world's largest producer of arrowroot starch, exporting to Britain and North America. As other starches replaced arrowroot, the industry gradually declined, but arrowroot starch is still a specialty of Saint Vincent, and the government has also tried to revive this traditional industry.
